content:
NASA's Perseverance Mars rover has driven farther than any vehicle ever has on the surface of another world. On Oct. 11, the rover's odometer reached 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers), eclipsing the record of 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) set by NASA's Opportunity rover, which explored Mars from 2004 to 2018.

Perseverance reached the mark on the 2,006th Martian day, or sol, of its mission — covering in five and a half years a distance that took Opportunity almost 15. A 299.6-foot (91.31-meter) drive on Oct. 11 pushed the rover past the record as it traveled toward an area called "Idubi" through the region off the western rim of Jezero Crater nicknamed "Lac de Charmes."

What makes the mileage remarkable is how it was earned. Nine out of every ten drives Perseverance makes follow a route the rover picks for itself. Its autonomous navigation system, AutoNav, takes stereo images of the terrain ahead, builds a 3D map, and selects the safest path toward its drive goal — continuously, thanks to a fast co-processor called the Vision Compute Element. Earlier rovers had to pause and "think" before each drive segment. Perseverance thinks while it rolls.

The destination matters as much as the distance. The rocks and terrain of Lac de Charmes are so ancient that their Earthly equivalents have long since been erased by erosion and plate tectonics — Mars has no tectonic plates — and Idubi is where the science team hopes to find traces of ancient hydrothermal systems. Jezero Crater is an ancient lakebed, and its crater rim may hold warm, watery underground environments where life could once have begun.

Perseverance's engineering hardware and instruments are in excellent shape, with all redundant systems still available, project manager Steven Lee of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory told Reuters. A recent assessment concluded the systems are capable of operating well into the 2030s, and the rover is showing no signs of slowing down.
